chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Harun ibn Muslim, from Mas'ada ibn Sadaqa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

There was a group of people in the presence of my father, and they differed regarding Al-Nabeez. Some of them said, 'The cup which intoxicates is prohibited.' And some of them said, 'A little of what intoxicates, and its lot is prohibited.' So they referred the matter to my father (peace be upon him). So my father said: 'Do you see the measure (qist)? If not for what is poured into it first, it would be full. And similarly, the other cup, if not for the first one, it would not intoxicate.'

He (the narrator) said, 'Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever enters one vein from his veins with a little of what a lot of it would intoxicate, Allah will punish that vein with three hundred and sixty types from the types of punishment.'.

key_terms.النَّبِيذ: Al-Nabeez (a specific type of fermented drink)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Al-Nabeez and the principle of intoxication in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia juristic principle of 'Kathiruhu Yuskiru Qaliluhu' (the intoxicating quantity determines the ruling for the small quantity) through Imam al-Sadiq’s analogy of a measuring vessel, clarifying that the presence of the intoxicant itself, rather than its volume, dictates prohibition. It reinforces the severity of minor consumption by citing a Prophetic tradition warning of specific divine punishments for the veins carrying the intoxicant, a concept central to Shia fiqh regarding khamr. This discussion highlights the methodological rigor in distinguishing between the substance's nature and its measurable effects.
